query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, the phase stability across extreme environments is primarily governed by the Al content setting the local lattice distortion and stacking fault energy. An optimal range of Al content promotes a moderately distorted single-phase FCC matrix that resists the formation of unwanted brittle intermetallic precipitates at high temperatures and under irradiation while enabling deformation twinning at cryogenic temperatures for improved toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic or near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy produced under standard casting or additive manufacturing conditions, exhibiting a single FCC solid-solution phase.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the Al content (while keeping Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni constant) to compare samples with lower-than-optimal, optimal, and higher-than-optimal Al concentrations.
generation.conditions: The tests are conducted under controlled thermal conditions spanning cryogenic temperatures (e.g., 77 K) and high temperatures (e.g., 800 °C), as well as under simulated radiation exposure and oxidizing atmospheres to assess environmental resistance.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortion and the resultant stacking fault energy of the FCC matrix, which mediate the onset of deformation twinning and suppress deleterious phase segregation.
generation.mechanism: Al atoms, due to their larger size and specific electronic interactions, modulate the lattice distortion and lower the stacking fault energy when present in an optimal range. This tuning allows the alloy to maintain a single-phase solid solution and simultaneously trigger deformation twinning under cryogenic loading, while also limiting atomic diffusion that would otherwise promote secondary phase precipitation under high-temperature or irradiated conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline equiatomic composition, alloys with the optimal Al content will exhibit (a) fewer or delayed secondary intermetallic precipitations during high-temperature aging, (b) enhanced retention of high-temperature strength and corrosion/oxidation resistance, (c) reduced radiation-induced segregation or defect coalescence, and (d) improved cryogenic toughness due to the activation of deformation twinning mechanisms.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the standard equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni composition processed under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies only when the other elemental concentrations are held constant (or nearly so) and under processing conditions that yield equilibrium or near-equilibrium microstructures. It may not hold if non-equilibrium processing or drastic changes in other elements occur.
generation.uncertainty: Precise quantitative relationships between the Al concentration, stacking fault energy, and each performance property are not fully established; additional parametric studies and simulations are needed to correlate the microscopic energy scales with macroscopic property changes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA samples where the Al content is systematically varied (e.g., low, optimal, and high relative to the equiatomic baseline) while keeping all other elemental percentages constant. Subject these samples to high-temperature aging, radiation exposure, and cryogenic tensile tests. Characterize phase composition and microstructure using X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy, and estimate stacking fault energy through both theoretical calculations and slip-system analysis.
measurements: Quantitative phase analysis (e.g., XRD peak breadth, TEM observation of secondary phases)
Mechanical testing (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, ductility) at cryogenic and elevated temperatures
Assessment of radiation-induced defect density via microscopy or spectroscopy
Evaluation of oxidation/corrosion resistance through weight gain or surface analysis after high-temperature exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If varying the Al content does not yield systematic changes in the lattice distortion/stacking fault energy (as evidenced by similar microstructural features and deformation mechanisms across compositions) or fails to correlate with improvements in preventing secondary phase formation, retaining high-temperature strength, sustaining radiation tolerance, and enhancing cryogenic toughness relative to the baseline, then the hypothesized mechanism is falsified.

AbstractThe interface between high-performance thermoelectric materials and electrodes critically governs the conversion efficiency and long-term reliability of thermoelectric generators under high-temperature operation. Here, we propose AlxCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys (HEA) as barrier layers to bond Cu-W electrodes with p-type skutterudite (p-SKD) thermoelectric materials. The HEA/p-SKD interface exhibited excellent chemical bonding with a stable and controllable reaction layer, forming a dense, defect-free (Fe,Ni,Co,Cr)Sb phase (thickness of ~2.5 μm) at the skutterudites side. The interfacial resistivity achieved a low value of 0.26 μΩ·cm2 and remained at 7.15 μΩ·cm2 after aging at 773 K for 16 days. Moreover, the interface demonstrated remarkable mechanical stability, with an initial shear strength of 88 MPa. After long-term aging for 16 days at 773 K, the shear strength retained 74 MPa (only 16% degradation), ranking among the highest reported for thermoelectric materials/metal joints.
